ate.e: Probably a remodelling of earlier eat by analogy with other strong verbs such as break:†brake, give:gave, speak:†spake; compare the same process in rare Middle English at (“ate”) besides more usual et. However, the pronunciation /ɛt/ likely continues Middle English et, from Old English ǣt, from Proto-West Germanic *āt.

athirst.e: From Middle English athirst, from Old English ofþyrst, past participle of ofþyrstan (“to smart from thirst”), equivalent to a- (“of”, Etymology 8) + thirst (verb).

atone.e: From atone (“reconciled”), from Middle English atone, attone, atoon (“agreed”, literally “at one”), equivalent to at + one. Regarding the different phonological development of atone and one, see the note in one.
atone.g: To make reparation, compensation, amends or satisfaction for an offence, crime, mistake or deficiency.

atonement.e: Perhaps from atone + -ment as translation of Medieval Latin adūnāmentum; however, the noun is found earlier than the verb (atone); and in this light, the proper etymology is at + onement.
atonement.g: Making amends to restore a damaged relationship; expiation.

atrocity.e: From Middle French atrocité, from Latin atrōcitās, from atrōx (“terrible, cruel”) + -tās, from āter (“matte black”).
atrocity.g: An extremely cruel act; a horrid act of injustice.

attach.e: From Middle English attachen, from Old French atachier, variant of estachier (“bind”), derived from estache (“stick”), from Frankish *stakkā, *stakō (“stick”), from Proto-Germanic *stakô (“pole, bar, stick, stake”).
attach.g: To fasten, to join to (literally and figuratively).

attack.e: Borrowed from French attaque, derived from the verb attaquer, from Italian attaccare (“to join, attach”) (used in attaccare battaglia (“to join battle”)), from Frankish *stakkijan (“to stick, stick to, attach”).
attack.g: An attempt to cause damage, injury to, or death of an opponent or enemy.

attempt.e: Late 14th century, as Middle English attempten, from Old French atempter, from Latin attemptō (“to try, solicit”), from ad- (“to”) + temptō; see tempt. By surface analysis, at- + tempt.

attend.e: From Middle English attenden, atenden (“to devote oneself (to a task, etc.); to pay attention to (something), to look after; to consider (something); to expect or look forward to (something); to intend to do (something); to help or serve (someone), attend upon; to take care of (something)”), from Old French atendre (“to await, wait for; to expect.
attend.g: Senses relating to caring for or waiting on someone, or accompanying or being present.

attendance.e: From Middle English attendance, from Old French atendance, from atendre (“to attend, listen”).
attendance.g: The act of attending; the state of being present; presence.

attendant.e: From Middle English attendant, attendaunt, from Old French attendant. By surface analysis, attend + -ant.
attendant.g: One who attends; one who works with or watches over someone or something.

attention.e: From Middle English attencioun, borrowed from Latin attentio, attentionis, from attendere, past participle attentus (“to attend, give heed to”); see attend. Equivalent to attend + -tion.

attentive.e: From Middle English attentif, attentijf, from Old French attentif.
attentive.g: Paying attention; noticing, watching, listening, or attending closely.

attentively.e: From Middle English attentifly, attentifli, equivalent to attentive + -ly.

attest.e: PIE word tréyes Borrowed from Middle French attester, from Latin attestor (“to witness to, bear witness”), from at-, combining form of ad (“to”) + testor (“to bear witness”), from testis (“a witness”).
attest.g: To affirm to be correct, true, or genuine.

attitude.e: From French attitude, from Italian attitudine (“attitude, aptness”), from Medieval Latin aptitūdō (“aptitude”) and actitūdō (“acting, posture”), from Latin aptō and actitō.
attitude.g: The position of the body or way of carrying oneself.

attract.e: From Latin attractus, past participle of attrahere (“to draw to, attract”), from ad (“to”) + trahere (“to draw”).

attribute.g: A characteristic or quality of a thing.
